title: Cover and Drop
premise: Juniper Dravenmoor, a fixer for the Meridian Office — an embassy that exists on no map and in no treaty — discovers their long-term safe house has been listed on a real estate site, interior photos included, down to the hidden documents drawer. Someone inside the Office is selling them out, and the listing is a message: come negotiate, or be exposed. Juniper assembles the ragtag household of misfit operatives who have become their only family to trace the leak, uncovering that the 'secret worth killing for' is a ledger proving the Office manufactured the crisis that created all of them. In the end, Juniper trades the ledger to a rival intelligence service not for money or immunity, but for new identities for everyone in the house — burning the Office's fiction to the ground so their found family can finally live visible, ordinary lives.
about_author: Cyrus Ishikawa is the pen name of a former logistics consultant who spent a decade moving sensitive cargo through three continents before turning to fiction. They write from an undisclosed coastal city, specializing in thrillers about people whose jobs officially never happened.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. While running a routine errand, Juniper finds the safe house — their home of twelve years — listed online with interior photos, including the false drawer behind the bookshelf. The emotional beat is cold dread: invisibility was the only rule that mattered, and someone just broke it deliberately.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper gathers the household: cryptographer Wren, ex-medic Okafor, teenage hacker Sable, and paranoid quartermaster Devi. They debate evacuating versus staying. The beat is reluctant family: they argue like siblings because leaving each other has never been on the table.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A flashback-heavy chapter tracing how each resident arrived at the safe house broken and was rebuilt by routine. Wren realizes the listing photos were taken over months, meaning the traitor had long access. The beat is tender melancholy undercut by rising suspicion of everyone.

chapters.title: Contact Protocol
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper reaches out to the Meridian Office through dead-drop channels and receives only one reply: a realtor's open-house invitation for Saturday. The beat is humiliation sharpening into resolve — the Office isn't protecting them; it's herding them.

chapters.title: Open House
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Posing as buyers, Sable and Devi attend the open house and identify the agent's handler by his shoes: Meridian-issue. They also find a camera feeding somewhere off-site. The beat is adrenaline and dark comedy, two spies pretending to care about countertops.

chapters.title: What the Drawer Held
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. The team inventories what the photographed drawer exposed and confronts the truth: it held the ledger — proof the Office engineered the war that orphaned its own operatives. The beat is betrayal deepening into purpose; this secret explains why they were all collected.

chapters.title: The Rewritten Rules
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. Devi digs into twelve years of shifting protocols and maps them against Office leadership changes, concluding Director Hale has been cleaning house — literally. The beat is grim clarity: every rule rewrite was a trap snapping shut one notch at a time.

chapters.title: Sable Runs
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Terrified, seventeen-year-old Sable bolts to a former contact and accidentally leads a surveillance team back toward the house. Juniper extracts them violently. The beat is fear and guilt — the family's weakest link nearly dooms them all, and knows it.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Hale offers Juniper a deal: surrender the ledger, retire quietly, and the others get pensions. Alone, Juniper almost takes it. The beat is temptation — survival offered at the price of abandoning the only people who ever stayed.

chapters.title: The Vote
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Juniper confesses the offer to the household. Instead of voting to scatter, they vote unanimously to fight and use the ledger themselves. The beat is belonging crystallizing into courage: found family choosing each other over safety, together.

chapters.title: Counter-Offer
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. The team approaches Voss, a rival service officer with old debts to Juniper, offering the ledger for five new identities. Voss is interested but demands verification — and warns them Hale has a kill team already inbound. The beat is wary alliance, trust extended across enemy lines.

chapters.title: Ghost Traffic
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable traces the open-house camera feed to a Meridian black site and, more importantly, finds evidence Hale fabricated the original crisis file. The beat is vindication — the teenager who always felt least belongs proves indispensable.

chapters.title: Safe House No More
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. The kill team hits the house while most are out; Devi stays behind to burn the archives and barely escapes through the crawlspace she installed years ago. The beat is loss and survival — the home is gone, but the family walks out intact.

chapters.title: Scattered
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Regrouping in a motel, the team is demoralized, hunted, and short on options. Juniper admits they've been following rewritten rules for years without asking who writes them. The beat is rock bottom transformed into clarity: stop playing defense.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Third Copy
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reveals she made a third copy years ago, hidden in plain sight inside the listing itself — steganographic data embedded in the real estate photos. The traitor unknowingly distributed their insurance. The beat is triumphant irony: the weapon used against them becomes their shield.

chapters.title: Identifying the Photographer
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Photo metadata and habit analysis point to the mole: not a stranger, but Marlowe, the Office liaison who delivered their groceries and medicine for a decade. The beat is heartbreak — the kindest face in their orbit was the cage's architect.

chapters.title: Marlowe
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper confronts Marlowe, who claims he photographed the house to force the Office's hand and protect the residents from a purge he saw coming. Juniper must decide whether he's a traitor, an ally, or both. The beat is moral vertigo — even betrayal can wear a caretaker's face.

chapters.title: Exchange Terms
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Final negotiation with Voss: the verified ledger plus Sable's evidence of Hale's fabrication, in exchange for identities, passage, and public release of the file if anything happens to the family. The beat is hard-bargained hope — leverage finally on their side.

chapters.title: Hale's Last Rule
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Hale corners Juniper personally, offering everything again — then revealing the purge order includes the whole household regardless. Juniper stalls him while the exchange executes elsewhere. The beat is cold fury meeting calm sacrifice; Juniper keeps him talking with the same patience the Office once taught them.

chapters.title: Cover and Drop
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. The exchange goes live: ledger to Voss, identities confirmed, the fabrication file released simultaneously to three news agencies. Hale's kill team stands down as exposure makes them liabilities. The beat is breathless convergence — every thread pulling taut at once.

chapters.title: Afterimages
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Fallout: Hale arrested by his own institution, Marlowe vanished with a pension and a clear conscience, the Meridian Office quietly dissolved. The family mourns the house that wasn't safe but was still home. The beat is grief braided with relief — survival cost something after all.

chapters.title: A Visible Life
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Months later, in a coastal town under new names, the household unpacks boxes in an ordinary house with nothing hidden in any drawer. Juniper plants a garden where a dead drop used to be. The final beat is belonging fulfilled: they traded the secret worth killing for the right to be seen.
